methods.label: Count elapsed days in whole weeks
methods.explanation:
Two dates fall on the same weekday exactly when the number of days between them is a multiple of \(7\). Let \(L\) be the number of days in year \(N\). From its \(300\)th day to the \(200\)th day of year \(N+1\), the elapsed time is
\[
(L-300)+200=L-100.
\]
A year has \(365\) or \(366\) days, so this difference is \(265\) or \(266\). Since
\[
265=37\cdot7+6,
\qquad 266=38\cdot7,
\]
the two Tuesdays force \(L=366\). Thus year \(N\) is a leap year, and its preceding year \(N-1\) has \(365\) days because consecutive years cannot both be leap years.

From the \(100\)th day of year \(N-1\) to the \(300\)th day of year \(N\), the elapsed time is
\[
(365-100)+300=565=80\cdot7+5
\]
days. Therefore Tuesday is five weekdays after the requested day. Five days before Tuesday is \(\boxed{\text{Thursday}}\), choice A.

candidate.annotationRationale: Weekday equality is a divisibility condition on elapsed-day differences, so integer remainder reasoning is the target even without formal congruence notation. Calendar year lengths and leap-year facts supply the context, while multiples support the seven-day calculations.

review.mathematicalCheck: The two Tuesdays are L-100 days apart. Of 265 and 266, only 266 is divisible by 7, forcing year N to be leap and its preceding year to have 365 days. The requested date is 565=80·7+5 days before Tuesday, hence Thursday.
